videos.title: How Tiny Houses Are Built, Start to Finish
videos.oneLine: A builder walks through framing, wiring and insulating a 20 square meter house on a trailer.
summary: A two-person team builds a 20 square meter house on a trailer in six weeks.
The main idea: weight decides everything, from the frame to the kitchen counter.
They frame in light steel, then add windows, wiring and a sheep wool insulation.
It ends on the costs, and the three things they would change next time.
For anyone planning a tiny house who wants to see the order of the work.

keyPoints.text: Every choice starts with one question: how much does it weigh?
Light steel framing is about a third lighter than timber for the same strength.
Fewer, bigger windows: every frame adds weight and a place to leak.
Plan every socket on paper before a single cable goes in.
Sheep wool insulation breathes and handles damp better than foam.
About 31,000 euros in materials, and a lot of weekends.
Next time: a bigger door, the loft ladder moved, more storage under the floor.

quotes.text: A small house isn't a small project. It's every project, squeezed into less room.
Build the smallest version of everything first. You can always add, you can rarely take away.

clips.why: Why steel beats timber, said simply, with the cutting on screen.
The three changes they would make. A list that stands on its own.

videos.title: Pricing Your First Product (Without Guessing)
videos.oneLine: Three ways to set a first price, and why charging too little is the more common mistake.
summary: A maker explains how to set the first price for something you sell.
Three ways in: what it costs you, what it is worth to the buyer, and what they pay today.
Most first prices are too low, and a low price is harder to raise than a high one to lower.
It ends on a simple test: ask ten people, and raise the price until two say no.
For anyone about to sell their first product or service.

keyPoints.text: Most first prices are picked to feel safe, and end up too low.
Cost plus gives you the floor, never the ceiling.
Value pricing: what the buyer saves or gains, not what it costs you.
What they pay today is your real competitor, often a spreadsheet.
A low price is harder to raise than a high one is to lower.
Test: ask ten people, raise the price until two say no.

quotes.text: That's your real competitor. Not the other startup. The spreadsheet.
Your first price isn't forever. It's your first guess, made on purpose.

clips.why: Why charging too little hurts, in under a minute and a half.
The ten-people test, start to finish.

videos.title: Sourdough for Beginners: Your First Loaf
videos.oneLine: A first sourdough loaf in five steps, with the one thing most beginners rush.
summary: A baker walks through a first sourdough loaf in five steps.
The starter has to be lively first: it should double within six hours of a feed.
Mix, rest, then fold four times instead of kneading.
The step beginners rush is the rise. Go by the look of the dough, not the clock.
For a first loaf at home, with no special tools beyond a pot with a lid.

keyPoints.text: Your starter is ready when it doubles within six hours of a feed.
Rest the flour and water for half an hour before adding anything else.
Fold four times, half an hour apart, instead of kneading.
Judge the rise by the dough, not the clock: about half again, full of air.
Bake in a lidded pot: 20 minutes lid on, 20 minutes lid off.

quotes.text: Don't watch the clock. Watch the dough.
That's your first loaf. The second one will be better.

clips.why: The rise, the step beginners rush, explained in one minute.
